title: Our altars and statues are within
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα δὲ ὁ Κέλσος φησὶν ἡμᾶς βωμοὺς καὶ ἀγάλματα καὶ νεὼς ἱδρύεσθαι φεύγειν, ἐπεὶ τὸ πιστὸν ἡμῖν ἀφανοῦς καὶ ἀποῤῥήτου κοινωνίας οἴεται εἶναι σύνθημα· οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι βωμοὶ μέν εἰσιν ἡμῖν τὸ ἑκάστου τῶν δικαίων ἡγεμονικὸν, ἀφ᾿ οὗ ἀναπέμπεται ἀληθῶς καὶ νοητῶς εὐώδη „θυμιάματα,“ „προσευχαὶ“ ἀπὸ συνειδήσεως καθαρᾶς. διὸ λέγεται παρὰ τῷ Ἰωάννῃ ἐν τῇ Ἀποκαλύψει· „τὰ δὲ θυμιάματά εἰσιν αἱ προσευχαὶ τῶν ἁγίων“ καὶ παρὰ τῷ ὑμνῳδῷ· „γενηθήτω ἡ προσευχή μου ὡς θυμίαμα ἐνώπιόν δου.“ ἀγάλματα δὲ καὶ πρέποντα θεῷ ἀναθήματα, οὐχ ὑπὸ βαναύσων τεχνιτῶν κατεσκευασμένα· ἀλλ᾿ ὑπὸ λόγου θεοῦ τρανούμενα καὶ μορφούμενα ἐν ἡμῖν. αἱ ἀρεταὶ, μιμήματα τυγχάνουσαι τοῦ πρωτοτόκου „πάσης κτίσεως.“ ἐν ᾧ ἐστι δικαιοσύνης καὶ σωφροσύνης καὶ ἀνδρείας καὶ σοφίας καὶ εὐσεβείας καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἀρετῶν παραδείγματα. ἐν πᾶσιν οὖν ἐστι, τοῖς κατὰ τὸν θεῖον λόγον σωφροσύνην ἑαυτοῖς κατασκευάσασι καὶ δικαιοσύνην καὶ ἀνδρείαν καὶ σοφίαν καὶ εὐσέβειαν καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἀρετῶν τὰ κατασκευάσματα, ἀγάλματα· οἷς πρέπον εἶναι πεπείσμεθα τιμᾶσθαι τὸ πρωτότυπον πάντων ἀγαλμάτων. τὴν εἰκόνα „τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου.“ τὸν μονογενῆ θεόν. ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ ἐκδυόμενοι „τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον σὺν ταῖς πράξεσιν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐνδυόμενοι τὸν νέον. τὸν ἀνακαινούμενον εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν κατ᾿ εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος αὐτὸν,“ τὸ „κατ᾿ εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος“ εἶναι ἀναλαμβάνοντες. ἀγάλματα ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ποιοῦσιν, ὁποῖα βούλεται ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸς, ἐκείνου. ὥσπερ δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀγαλματοποιῶν οἱ μέν τινες εἰσὶ θαυμαστῶς κατορθοῦντες τὸ ἔργον, ὥσπερ εἰπεῖν Φειδίας ἢ Πολύκλειτος ἢ ζωγράφοι Ζεῦξις καὶ Ἀπελλῆς, ἕτεροι δὲ ἔλαττον τούτων ἀγαλματοποιοῦσι, καὶ ἄλλοι ἔτι καὶ τῶν δευτέρων ἔλαττον, καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς πολλὴ διαφορά ἐστι τῆς τῶν ἀγαλμάτων καὶ εἰκόνων κατασκευῆς· τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον οἱ μέν τινες εἰσὶ ποιοῦντες ἀγάλματα τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεοῦ βέλτιον καὶ κατὰ τελείαν ἐπιστήμην, ὡς μηδεμίαν εἶναι σύγκρισιν τοῦ ὑπὸ Φειδίου κατασκευασθέντος Ὀλυμπίου Διὸς πρὸς τὸν κατασκευασθέντα „κατ᾿ εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος“ θεοῦ· πάντων δὲ τῶν ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ κτίσει πολλῷ βέλτιον καὶ ὑπερέχον ἐστὶν ἐν τῷ σωτῆρι ἡμῶν, τῷ λέγοντι· „ὁ πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοί.“
pass_a_gloss: After these things Celsus says we flee (φεύγω) from setting up (ἱδρύω) altars (βωμοί) and statues (ἀγάλματα) and temples (νεῴ), since he thinks the pledge (τὸ πιστόν) of an unseen (ἀφανής) and unspeakable/secret (ἀπόρρητος) fellowship (κοινωνία) is for us a token (σύνθημα); not seeing that altars for us are the ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν) of each of the righteous (δίκαιοι), from which are sent up (ἀναπέμπω) truly and intelligibly (νοητῶς) sweet-smelling (εὐώδης) incense (θυμιάματα), prayers (προσευχαί) from a pure (καθαρός) conscience (συνείδησις). Therefore it is said by John in the Apocalypse: the incense is the prayers of the saints (ἅγιοι); and by the hymn-singer (ὑμνῳδός): let my prayer become (γίνομαι) as incense before you. But statues and offerings (ἀναθήματα) fitting (πρέπω) to God, not furnished by vulgar (βάναυσος) craftsmen (τεχνῖται) but articulated (τρανόω) and formed (μορφόω) in us by the Word of God, [are] the virtues (ἀρεταί), being imitations (μιμήματα) of the firstborn (πρωτότοκος) of all creation (κτίσις); in whom are patterns (παραδείγματα) of righteousness and temperance (σωφροσύνη) and courage (ἀνδρεία) and wisdom and piety (εὐσέβεια) and the remaining virtues. In all, then, who according to the divine word have furnished (κατασκευάζω) for themselves temperance and righteousness and courage and wisdom and piety and the constructions (κατασκευάσματα) of the remaining virtues, there are statues; by which we are persuaded (πείθω) it is fitting the prototype (πρωτότυπον) of all statues be honoured (τιμάω): the image (εἰκών) of the invisible (ἀόρατος) God, the only-begotten (μονογενής) God. But also those stripping off (ἐκδύομαι) the old man with his deeds (πράξεις) and putting on (ἐνδύομαι) the new, the one being renewed (ἀνακαινόω) into full knowledge (ἐπίγνωσις) according to the image of the one who created (κτίζω) him, taking up (ἀναλαμβάνω) being 'according to the image of the creator', make in themselves statues of that one, of what sort the God over all wishes (βούλομαι). And just as among statue-makers (ἀγαλματοποιοί) some are wonderfully succeeding (κατορθόω) in the work, as for instance Phidias or Polyclitus, or painters (ζωγράφοι) Zeuxis and Apelles, and others make statues less than these, and others still less even than the second, and in short (ἁπαξαπλῶς) there is much difference (διαφορά) in the making (κατασκευή) of statues and images; in the same way some are making statues of the God over all better and according to perfect (τέλειος) knowledge (ἐπιστήμη), so that there is no comparison (σύγκρισις) of the Olympian Zeus furnished by Phidias to the one furnished according to the image of the creating God; and much better and surpassing (ὑπερέχω) all those in the whole creation is the one in our Saviour, who says: the Father [is] in me.
pass_b_english: After this Celsus says that we shun setting up altars and statues and temples, since he supposes that this is the token by which we keep faith with a hidden and secret fellowship. He does not see that our altars are the ruling mind of each righteous person, from which there truly and spiritually rises fragrant “incense”: “prayers” from a pure conscience. That is why John says in the Revelation: “The incense is the prayers of the saints” (Revelation 5:8); and the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2).

Statues, and offerings fit for God, are with us not made by common artisans. They are given clear shape and form in us by the Word of God: they are the virtues, which are likenesses of “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15). In him are the patterns of righteousness and self-control and courage and wisdom and piety and the other virtues. In all, then, who in keeping with the divine Word have fashioned in themselves self-control and righteousness and courage and wisdom and piety, and the works of the other virtues, there are statues. With these, we are convinced, it is fitting to honour the original of all statues: “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), the only-begotten God (John 1:18).

Moreover, those who put off “the old self with its deeds and put on the new, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of the one who created it” (Colossians 3:9–10), taking up the state of being “after the image of the Creator,” make within themselves statues of him, such as the God over all wishes.

Among sculptors some achieve their work marvellously, such as Phidias or Polyclitus, or among painters Zeuxis and Apelles; others make statues less well than these, and others again less well than those of the second rank; and, in a word, there is great difference in the making of statues and images. In the same way some make statues of the God over all better than others, and with perfect knowledge, so that there is no comparison between the Olympian Zeus that Phidias made and the one fashioned after the image of God the Creator (Colossians 3:10). But far better than all those in the whole creation, and surpassing them, is the statue in our Saviour, who says: “The Father is in me” (John 14:11).

choices.choice: Celsus’s charge is reported, not quoted, so it is not put in quotation marks. τὸ πιστόν ... σύνθημα (‘the token of the pledge’) is rendered ‘the token by which we keep faith with’, and the same wording returns at the end of 8.20 where Origen repeats the charge. νοητῶς (‘to the mind’, as opposed to the senses) is rendered ‘spiritually’. Psalm 140:2 in the Septuagint is Psalm 141:2 in English Bibles; the Septuagint γενηθήτω is rendered ‘Let my prayer be’, not the Hebrew-based ‘be set forth’; the source’s δου is a typographic slip for σου. Revelation 5:8 reads ‘golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints’; Origen gives the gist (compare Revelation 8:3-4). ‘From a pure conscience’ may echo 1 Timothy 3:9 or 2 Timothy 1:3; not cited inline. βάναυσοι τεχνῖται is rendered ‘common artisans’ (manual tradesmen), and τρανούμενα ‘given clear shape’. κατὰ τὸν θεῖον λόγον is rendered ‘in keeping with the divine Word’ (κατά, not agency) and capitalised as the Word who forms the virtues in us (stated two sentences earlier); it could also mean ‘divine reason’ or ‘divine teaching’. ‘The only-begotten God’ follows the reading μονογενὴς θεός at John 1:18. Colossians 3:9-10 is quoted with ἄνθρωπον in the Greek (‘old man’); rendered ‘old self’ in modern English, with ‘it’ for the new self. In ἀγάλματα ... ποιοῦσιν, ὁποῖα βούλεται ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸς, ἐκείνου the genitive ἐκείνου (‘of him’) is left as ‘statues of him’; it may refer to the Creator or to the image just named, and the English keeps that open. In the comparison with Phidias’ Zeus, the masculine τὸν κατασκευασθέντα has no expressed noun (it may mean the statue or the renewed man) and is rendered ‘the one fashioned’; θεοῦ is taken with τοῦ κτίσαντος (‘God the Creator’), and because Origen adds θεοῦ to the Pauline words the phrase is cited to Colossians 3:10 without quotation marks. The final clause has no expressed noun; the neuter βέλτιον καὶ ὑπερέχον points to ἄγαλμα, so ‘the statue’ is supplied. ‘The Father is in me’ matches John 14:11 (also John 10:38, 14:10).

Psalm 141:2: Hebrew-based 'be set forth' replaced by LXX 'be as incense'

κατὰ τὸν θεῖον λόγον 'in keeping with', not agency 'by'
